title: 2016 AMC 12A Problem 18
statement: For some positive integer \(n,\) the number \(110n^3\) has \(110\) positive integer divisors, including \(1\) and the number \(110n^3.\) How many positive integer divisors does the number \(81n^4\) have?

solutions.text:
The number \(110n^3\) is divisible by the three distinct primes \(2,5,11.\) If its prime exponents are \(r_1,r_2,\ldots,\) then \((r_1+1)(r_2+1)\cdots=110,\) where \(110=2\cdot5\cdot11.\) Because there are already at least three factors greater than \(1,\) there are exactly three, so no other prime divides \(n.\)

Each exponent in \(110n^3\) is \(1\pmod3,\) so each divisor-count factor \(r_i+1\) is \(2\pmod3.\) The factors \(2,5,11\) all have that form, so the exponents are \(1,4,10\) in some order. After subtracting the exponent \(1\) from \(110\) and dividing by \(3,\) the exponents in \(n\) are \(0,1,3\) in some order. Thus \(n=pq^3\) for two distinct primes \(p,q\) chosen from \(2,5,11.\)

Consequently \(n^4\) has exponents \(4\) and \(12,\) while \(81=3^4\) introduces a third prime because \(n\) is not divisible by \(3.\) Hence the number of divisors of \(81n^4\) is \[ \begin{gathered} (4+1)(4+1)(12+1)\\ =5\cdot5\cdot13\\ =325. \end{gathered} \]

Thus, the correct answer is D.
